newsitem.title: USA: U.S. critical of libel law use in Singapore.
newsitem.headline: U.S. critical of libel law use in Singapore.

text.p: The United States reacted cautiously to a large libel damages award on Thursday against an opposition politician in Singapore but said it had previously criticised use of defamation laws in political cases there.

The State Department said it did not have "any particular comment" on a Singapore court's award of a record Singapore $8.08 million (US$5.65 million) to Prime Minister Goh Chok Tong and colleagues after a political foe called them liars.

But spokesman John Dinger said the State Department's 1996 human rights report "is critical of the fact that in Singapore government leaders sometimes use defamation suits or the threat of such actions to discourage public criticism."

Dinger noted that there had been previous cases, including one involving the International Herald Tribune newspaper in 1995 over an article about Asian governments. "We're on the record as being critical of that practice," he said.

Singapore Justice Chao Hick Tin said Goh and his colleagues were justified in calling opposition politician Tang Liang Hong "an anti-English education, anti-Christian Chinese chauvinist" who was a danger to Singapore's racial harmony.

Tang had made "malicious" attacks on Goh, former prime minister Lee Kuan Yew and the others which could have affected "their moral authority to govern," including calling them liars over the chauvinism charge, Chao said in his judgment.
